set.rappels: About 9-10 short rappels on a single 60 m rope down the North Face line to Burgundy Col
set.rappel_count_note: Action Potential has no rappel line of its own. Parties finish into North Face terrain near Burgundy Ledge and take that route's descent. On one 60 m rope the descent works, but it takes many shorter rappels and some easy downclimbing rather than a few long ones; parties on a single rope have logged 9-10 to reach Burgundy Col. From the heavily slung summit boulder, a single 60 m rope comes up about 10 ft short of the only bolted anchor on the route, so use the intermediate station on the slab variation to reach Burgundy Ledge, or carry a 70 m rope. At the left end of Burgundy Ledge two stations sit above the fourth pitch, and one 60 m rope reaches from the upper one to the next station below. Several rappels use most of the rope, so knot the ends and check that both reach the next station. Pulls snag easily on the ledges and loose rock sits on every stance. No station-by-station list for one rope is known, and per-station distances are not known.
set.descent_text: Action Potential tops out in two possible ways, and the descent depends on which finish you take: either climb up past an old bolt to the skyline and ramble class-5.7 terrain to the true summit, or finish by traversing Burgundy Ledge into the standard North Face route. Either way, the descent used by essentially all parties is the North Face's rappel line: on a single 60 m rope, plan on about 9-10 shorter rappels from the summit area back down the face, off a heavily slung summit boulder, bolts, slung horns and constrictions, to Burgundy Col, 5-10 minutes from Action Potential's own start. Anchors are a mix of slung boulders/horns and fixed bolts; watch for old webbing and be deliberate pulling ropes, since the face has ledges that catch the line. From the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach to the highway.

review.single_rope: One 60 m rope is enough on the North Face descent using the available stations (intermediate station on the slab variation, two stations above P4); a 70 m is nicer; 9-10 rappels logged on a single rope. No per-station list on one rope.
review.changed: Dropped the five two-rope stations (40-60 m) and all double-rope wording; stated the single-rope count as 9-10 and what one 60 m does and does not reach; rewrote the one descent_text sentence.

set.rappels: About 9-10 short rappels on a single 60 m rope back to Burgundy Col
set.rappel_count_note: A single 60 m rope is enough for this descent when you use the available stations, with some easy downclimbing between them; parties on one rope have logged 9-10 rappels in all. From the summit boulder, a single 60 m falls about 10 ft short of the bolted ledge anchor, so use the intermediate station on the center slab variation to reach Burgundy Ledge, or carry a 70 m rope. Traverse Burgundy Ledge to the top of the fourth pitch, where two stations sit at its left end, then keep rappelling the route; one 60 m reaches from the upper ledge station to the next one below. A few rappels use most of the rope, so knot the ends and check that both reach the next station. Ropes stick easily and loose rock sits on the ledges, so pull with care. No station-by-station list for one rope is known, and per-station distances are not known.
set.descent_text: From the summit, the descent is a series of rappels down the face back to Burgundy Col, then a reversal of the approach. On a single 60 m rope that is about 9-10 shorter rappels with some easy downclimbing between stances. From a large, heavily slung boulder at the summit the line drops down the middle of the upper face toward a bolted anchor on a ledge (a single 60 m falls about 10 ft short, so use the intermediate station on the slab variation, or carry a 70 m); the face below runs down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch — traverse the ledge to a constriction where slings back up the next anchor — then lower again over lichen-covered rock to a slung horn right of the ascent line, then to broad, scree-covered upper ledges — pull the rope carefully here, as there's real potential to snag it on the ledge system — and finally down over the lower scramble terrain, landing back at Burgundy Col where the route starts. Anchors are a mix of slung natural features (boulder, horn) and fixed bolts/webbing — inspect webbing before weighting it, since it's exposed to UV and can be old. Once at the base of the last rappel, reverse the Burgundy Col approach (down the loose scree, then the boot path past the flat bench and creek crossing) back to the highway pullout.

review.single_rope: Sources say a single 60 m rope is sufficient using the existing stations, and one party used a single 70 m; 9-10 rappels logged on one rope. No full one-rope station list.
review.changed: Dropped the two-rope table (40/55/55/40/60 m) and all double-rope wording; rewrote summary, note and descent_text for one 60 m rope.

set.rappels: About 9-10 short rappels on a single 60 m rope down the North Face line to Burgundy Col
set.rappel_count_note: Ultramega OK has no rappel line of its own - it is a Northeast Buttress route that merges into upper North Face terrain, and parties take the North Face descent. On one 60 m rope that descent takes about 9-10 shorter rappels with some easy downclimbing; from the summit boulder a single 60 m falls about 10 ft short of the only bolted anchor, so use the intermediate station on the slab variation to reach Burgundy Ledge, or carry a 70 m rope. Traverse Burgundy Ledge to the stations above the fourth pitch and continue down the route. Ropes snag easily on this face and loose material sits on the ledges. No station-by-station list for one rope is known, and per-station distances are not known.
set.descent_text: Ultramega OK has no independent, well-established rappel line of its own — it is a Northeast Buttress route whose last pitch finishes up an offwidth crack to the summit, though a party that loses the line high up can traverse ledges into upper North Face terrain (near Burgundy Ledge) and finish from there. From wherever the route is topped out, the standard way down is the North Face rappel descent, about 9-10 shorter rappels on a single 60 m rope: from a heavily slung summit boulder down the upper face toward a bolted ledge anchor (use the intermediate station on the slab variation, or carry a 70 m, since a single 60 m falls about 10 ft short); down lichen-covered rock to a huge ledge near a rock arch (traverse the ledge to a constriction with slings); on to a blue-slung horn; then to broad scree ledges (watch the rope pull here — lots of snag potential) and finally back to Burgundy Col. From the base of the raps, reverse the Burgundy Col approach back to the highway. A few parties describe instead downclimbing loose 3rd/4th-class terrain on Burgundy's east side back toward the col to avoid rappelling altogether, but this is opportunistic route-finding rather than an established descent, and is not recommended in the wet or for parties unfamiliar with the terrain.

review.single_rope: Same descent as the North Face: a single 60 m is sufficient using the available stations, 70 m is nicer; 9-10 rappels logged on one rope.
review.changed: Dropped the two-rope table and all double-rope wording; rewrote the descent_text rappel sentences for one rope.

set.rappels: Rappel the NW Chimney back to the moat on a single 60 m rope, building anchors from slung horns, chockstones and your own gear: there is no fixed hardware, and what tat exists is poor. No count is published; plan on several rappels, then reverse the CJ Couloir.
set.rappel_count_note: No party has published a rappel count, rope length or station list for this descent, so none is shown, and how far one rope reaches in the chimney is not known. Expect to build every anchor yourself in the NW Chimney and carry cord to leave behind.
set.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb/simul-climb back to the top of the technical pitches, then rappel the NW Chimney back down to the moat using gear anchors you build as you go (there is no fixed hardware on this route; plan on a single 60 m rope, though no station list is known). Traverse back to the C-J col and reverse the CJ Couloir (roughly 3,400 ft of downclimbing/rappelling on snow and ice) to the base near the Cascade River, then retrace the short bushwhack and road walk to the trailhead. Avoid the Doug Direct descent some older references mention off the col -- a firsthand trip report calls it a slower, no-safer heather-and-rock traverse than simply reversing the couloir.

review.single_rope: Searches found no beta on this descent: no count, no rope length. Single 60 m is stated as the default only.
review.changed: Removed 'double ropes' and 'bring doubles' wording; stated the single-rope default and that no count or reach is known; rewrote the one parenthetical in descent_text.

set.rappels: 4 rappels on a single 70 m rope down the North Face, the usual descent
set.rappel_count_note: The North Face is the preferred way down, at four rappels on one 70 m rope. The Kor-Ingalls line can also be rappelled on a single 70 m rope, but ropes stick easily there and the line is shared with parties still climbing, so it is the less favored choice. A single 50 m rope does not reach the ground. Individual rappel lengths are not documented.

review.single_rope: Four rappels of the North Face on a single 70 m; Kor-Ingalls also possible on a single 70 m but ropes stick; 70 m needed because a 60 m may not make the North Face.
review.changed: Removed the pair-of-70 m alternative; kept 70 m as the single rope because sources say it is needed; added sticking and rope-length cautions.

set.rappels: No established rappel line on the buttress; the descent is the south side, with one or two rappels on a single 60 m rope at the short crux face.
set.rappel_count_note: Descend the south side rather than reversing the buttress. The one or two rappels on the Southwest Face line use a rock horn with fixed slings and rings. Rappel lengths are not documented, and how far one rope reaches there is not known. Retreat from the buttress itself is by single-rope rappels from anchors you build.

review.single_rope: Southwest Face descent has one or two rappels; no length documented for one rope; 60 m default assumed.
review.changed: Removed the doubled-up 50 m ropes wording; kept the south-side descent and count; descent_text left alone.

set.rappels: No established rappel line; descend the south side, with one or two rappels on a single 60 m rope at the Southwest Face crux. Carry spare slings and rings to build bail anchors if you need to retreat off the lower pitches.
set.rappel_count_note: Retreat from mid-route is by single-rope rappels from anchors you build; none are documented, and rappel lengths on the south side are not documented either.
